How Hogman works

A pen is a private network for a group of people: its own encrypted mesh, its own DNS zone, standard web certificates, and its own member list. This page goes through each part, then follows a request from start to finish.

The parts · One request, start to finish · Joining · Who can reach what · Names · Certificates · Shares · Removing people · Hosted pens · Who sees what · Limits

The parts

Each pen runs four small services, in containers, with its own data folder on the host, plus the host's ACME challenge DNS server (ns1.hogman.network). Only the shared front door and each pen's UDP relay port are reachable from the internet; the rest answer only inside the mesh.

PartSoftwareJob
Control server and relayHeadscale Registers devices, hands out WireGuard keys, pushes the access policy and DNS settings to every device. Its built-in relay carries encrypted packets for devices that can't reach each other directly.
RegistrarHogman (Go) The ledger: members, roles, invites, devices, names, the audit log. Writes the access policy into Headscale, answers DNS for the pen's zone, keeps home.<zone>'s public certificate via CertMagic DNS-01, scopes share TXT/EAB requests, and serves the home page's API over a private Unix socket.
Home pageCaddy Serves home.yourpen.pens.hogman.network inside the mesh, where members manage devices and names and the keeper runs the pen.
The pen's own nodeTailscale client Puts the pen's DNS and home page at one address inside the mesh.

Exact versions are pinned in core/compose.yaml. Members' computers run Hogman's unprivileged Go client (hogman-join). Everything on the host runs non-root (uid 65532).

One request, start to finish

Bob is a member. Alice shared a photo folder as photos.smith.pens.hogman.network. Bob types that address into his browser:

  1. DNS. Bob's browser hands any address ending in .smith.pens.hogman.network to the pen's loopback proxy (its automatic proxy setting says so; every other address goes straight to the internet as usual). The connection asks the pen's DNS inside the mesh, and the registrar answers with the mesh IP of Alice's share, something like 100.80.12.7. hogman-join checks via tsnet WhoIs that the IP belongs to a live enrolled peer before dialing.
  2. Policy. Bob's laptop may connect to that address on port 443 because the policy says members' devices may reach servers over HTTPS, and Alice's share is a server. If Bob were suspended, his devices would simply not be in the policy and nothing would connect.
  3. Tunnel. The connection goes over WireGuard, Bob's device to Alice's, end to end. If a firewall blocks a direct path, it goes through the pen's relay as encrypted WireGuard ciphertext; the relay can't read it.
  4. TLS. The share presents a standard HTTPS certificate for photos.smith.pens.hogman.network issued to Alice's local CertMagic keypair. Bob's browser verifies it with his computer's normal operating-system trust store — no custom root certificate is ever installed — and shows the padlock.

A stranger typing the same address gets nowhere at step 1: ns1.hogman.network returns empty NODATA for any non-challenge query (zero A/AAAA records exist), and mesh IPs exist only inside the tunnel.

Joining

  1. The keeper makes an invite: a single-use token, valid for 7 days. The link looks like https://<pen>.gate.hogman.network/join#t=<token>. The part after # never leaves the browser except when the invite is redeemed.
  2. The link's page shows one command, which downloads hogman-join for your computer and runs it with the link.
  3. hogman-join checks /hogman/v1/network over standard HTTPS, verifies that the pen zone matches the gate host, and redeems the invite with the name you choose. (Legacy links carrying fp= from before public certificates are refused; old private-CA pens must be recreated.)
  4. It starts the pen's background connection: a small built-in client (Tailscale's tsnet) running as you, never as administrator, with a loopback proxy that carries only HTTPS to the pen's names (plain http:// redirects locally to HTTPS). Browsers use it through an automatic proxy setting; everything else on the computer, including any Tailscale of your own, is untouched.
  5. It verifies that your pen's home page loads over HTTPS using the system trust store, and you're in — with zero OS root CA prompts.

Details and options: Joining a pen.

Who can reach what

Every device is either personal (a member's laptop or phone) or a server (anything set up to host sites). The registrar rebuilds the access policy from its ledger every few seconds and whenever something changes. It is default deny, meaning nothing is allowed unless a rule says so:

DeviceAccepts connections fromCan connect to
PersonalNobodyThe pen's DNS and home page; every server, on HTTPS (443) only
ServerAny active member's device, on 443 onlyThe pen's services; other servers, on 443
Anything elseNobodyNothing

Sometimes the best security fix for a surface is just to delete the surface.

So Hogman carries HTTPS and nothing else: no ssh, no other ports, no joining a whole computer as a server. Things that serve the pen are shares, each a small device of its own. The policy lists device addresses, not tags. So suspending someone is just leaving their devices out (instant and reversible), and a device that somehow joined without going through the registrar is in no rule at all and can reach nothing.

Names

  • Each pen has its own zone, yourpen.pens.hogman.network. The registrar is the only DNS server resolving site addresses in it, and answers only inside the mesh. Public pen names are used once and never recycled (D-21).
  • Members claim names first come, first served, up to 50 each: blog.yourpen.pens.hogman.network. Each name points at one server.
  • Reserved: home, ns, ns[0-9]*, registrar, search, nodes, www, join, admin, _acme-challenge. Devices also get automatic names under nodes.yourpen.pens.hogman.network.
  • Your browsing outside the pen never touches the pen's DNS.

Certificates

  • No custom root certificates (D-18, D-22): Hogman uses standard web certificates trusted by every browser and operating system out of the box. Nothing is installed into your computer's trust store. (Running hogman-join update on a public pen removes any leftover private Hogman roots from earlier releases; pre-switchover pens must be recreated.)
  • Split-horizon ACME DNS-01: Shares and portals generate their own local TLS keypairs with CertMagic and prove name ownership by placing a temporary TXT record under _acme-challenge.<site>.<pen>.pens.hogman.network via the registrar's mesh API (/api/acme/txt) and the host's authoritative challenge-dns server.
  • Primary + fallback CAs: Let's Encrypt is primary (with ARI support); on CA rate limits or outages, CertMagic fails over automatically to Google Trust Services via single-use EAB credentials (/api/acme/eab), governed by strict CAA rules on pens.hogman.network.
  • Public trade-offs: Every issued certificate appears in public Certificate Transparency logs (hostnames only, never site contents, D-21). Also, hosted pens share pens.hogman.network until it is listed on the Public Suffix List, so use a separate browser profile for any pen you don't fully trust (D-19). See Architecture & security for details.

Shares

hogman-join share blog 3000 creates a small device of its own, a server, using Tailscale's tsnet inside the join tool. It names itself blog, gets a public HTTPS certificate via CertMagic DNS-01 (key held locally on your machine), and passes visitors to port 3000 on your computer (or serves a folder through Go's os.Root). Because the share is its own device, your laptop stays a personal device that accepts no connections, and nothing needs administrator rights or an open port. A server may only name itself, and write challenge TXT records only for names it owns. Guide: Putting things in your pen.

Removing people

Three levels, from lightest:

  • Remove a device: one lost or stolen laptop is cut off.
  • Suspend: all of a member's devices are left out of the policy. Everything else is kept, and resuming takes under a second.
  • The boot (kick): the registrar marks them removed and refuses them everything, revokes their unused device keys and the invites they made, deletes every device they own from Headscale, deletes their Headscale user, rewrites the policy, and retires their site names permanently so nobody can impersonate their sites. All of it is in the audit log.

Measured on a real Mac over a home network: suspend 2.0 s, resume 0.8 s, the boot 2.1 s. What it can't do: take back data they already copied, or log them out of apps that keep their own accounts.

Hosted pens

On our server, every pen is its own set of the four containers above, with its own folder, database, keys, isolated Docker network (pen-<name>-core), and UDP relay port, using about 75 MB of memory. A shared front door (Caddy) holds ports 80 and 443 under a wildcard *.gate.hogman.network certificate, enforces a strict route allowlist, and passes each pen's control traffic only to that pen. Pens never share a network with each other.

Who sees what

The keeperUs (host control plane)
Who is in the pen, their devices, when they're onlineYesYes
Which pen names devices look upYesYes
What members send each other (WireGuard + TLS payloads)No (end to end encrypted)No
Your browsing outside the penNoNo
Could add a device or write a DNS-01 challengeVia UI/invitesYes, in principle (rogue certs appear in CT)

Hogman runs hosted pens only (D-24); joining a pen means trusting both its keeper and the host control plane not to mint rogue devices or DNS-01 challenges (which would be exposed in public Certificate Transparency logs).

Releases

Every compiled part of a release is built by GitHub from a public commit, never on someone's laptop. GitHub signs a record of which workflow and commit built each file (SLSA build provenance), and the release is published only if every file checks out. You can check any file yourself:

$ gh attestation verify hogman-join --repo celtiberi/hogman

The installer and hogman-join update check each download against its SHA-256 checksum, which catches broken downloads but trusts the server it came from. Signed updates, checked against a key built into Hogman, are planned.

Limits, honestly

  • Not independently audited. Young security software. Don't put anything high-stakes in a pen yet. Our own audit against the standard checklists (OWASP ASVS, CIS, SLSA), and what we fixed, is public.
  • Certificate Transparency logs (D-21): Pen and share hostnames appear in public CT logs when certificates are issued (never site contents).
  • Public Suffix List (D-19): pens.hogman.network is not on the PSL yet; use separate browser profiles across mutually untrusted pens.
  • Phones can't join yet; the app is in the works.
  • Windows is built but untested.
  • One control server per pen: if it's down, new connections, joins, DNS for the pen and certificate renewals stop. Existing direct connections keep working for a while.
